title: What is Express?
summary: Explains that Node is a general-purpose JavaScript runtime while Express is a web framework layered on top of it, built specifically for server back ends. Shows why Express replaces hand-written Node server code in almost every real project.

concepts.heading: Runtime vs framework
points: Node.js is strictly a runtime environment: it lets JavaScript run on a computer outside the browser. It is not a framework.
Express is a JavaScript framework that sits on top of Node and is aimed at one job, building the back end of a website.
Professional teams normally combine the two: Node supplies the runtime, Express supplies the structure for handling web requests.

concepts.heading: Why Express is needed
points: Node is general purpose. Beyond web back ends it is used for IoT devices and desktop apps (VS Code runs on Electron, which embeds Node), so it has no web-specific conveniences built in.
Express is a specialised tool for the web-server case: an electric screwdriver versus a plain one. Both can do the job; the specialised tool is faster for that one task.

A two-page site (home and about) written in bare Node needs a lot of low-level code that is hard to read. The same site in Express is short, modular and easy to follow, because Express talks to Node's internals for you.
Listed advantages: better readability, less code to write, and middleware, which lets you plug in features one piece at a time (covered in a later lesson).

concepts.heading: Popularity
points: Express is the default choice among JavaScript back-end frameworks, and State of JS usage statistics back this up.
That is why the course skips building a server with raw Node and goes straight to Express.

concepts.heading: (Extra) What Express removes
points: In bare Node you create a server with http.createServer, then branch on req.url and req.method by hand, set the status and Content-Type headers yourself with res.writeHead, and call res.end.

Express replaces that branching with one method call per route (app.get(path, handler)), sets sensible headers automatically in res.send, and returns a 404 'Cannot GET /path' page for unmatched routes without any extra code.
Express is itself built on Node's http module: app.listen creates an http.Server under the hood.
